title.title: Counterexamples to Ryser's covering conjecture
title.subtitle: Claim: intersecting $(q+1)$-partite hypergraphs with covering number $q+1$, for every large prime $q$

plain: Every two teams share a member: how many people must you pick to touch every team? More than Ryser bet

beats.text: Ryser: $r$-partite hypergraphs have covering number at most $r - 1$ times the matching number
The intersecting case was known for $r \le 5$; Aharoni proved $r = 3$ in 2001
The claim fails it at rank $q+1$, but nobody knows the smallest failing rank

steps: Start from a finite plane, one part per direction of lines
Randomly split and merge a few lines; edges still meet
A stability theorem rules out any cover of size $q$

achievement.label: Ryser's conjecture (Henderson 1971) and Gyárfás's tree cover
achievement.context: Built by perturbing the affine plane over $\mathbb F_q$; small ranks are untouched

verify.detail: Both main theorems: rank $q+1$ with balanced parts, and rank $s^n + 1$
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement; we did not build it

voice.text: When every two edges meet, Ryser bet one fewer than the parts would cover them.
Split a few lines of a finite plane at random; no small cover survives.
Claimed: counterexamples for every large prime.

sources.quote: the smallest counterexample rank is unknown
The thresholds are not explicit, so nobody knows the smallest rank at which Ryser actually fails. Small ranks are untouched.
